opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's a really interesting comparison, because people often point to flight simulators as evidence that simulation should just work for robots too. But there's an important asymmetry.

When a human pilot trains in a simulator, they already know an enormous amount about the real world. They've spent their whole lives walking around, picking things up, understanding physics, understanding cause and effect. So the simulator doesn't need to teach them what the world is like. It just needs to teach them a fairly narrow set of skills: which buttons to press, how to respond to an engine failure, what the procedures are. The pilot is filling in all the gaps between the simulation and reality with their own very rich prior knowledge. They know the simulator is an approximation, and they know *how* it's an approximation, so they can mentally correct for that.

A robot learning from simulated data doesn't have that. If the simulator is the main source of the model's understanding of the world, then whatever the simulator gets wrong, like contact dynamics, friction, deformable objects, the visual messiness of a real kitchen, the model just absorbs as truth. It has no independent grounding to tell it, "this part is fake, don't rely on it."

So I think the right way to see it is that simulation is most useful once you already have a model with a solid foundation of real-world experience. At that point, simulation can work more like it does for the pilot: a place to rehearse, explore rare situations, or practice something specific, while the model's real-world knowledge bridges the gap. But expecting simulation to supply the foundation itself is a lot like expecting someone who has never seen the physical world to learn everything about it from a video game. The pilot analogy works because the pilot isn't starting from zero, and that's exactly the part that's hard for robots.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts human real-world experience with a robot’s dependence on simulation, but it does not discuss models trained across multiple domains or say they lack inherent knowledge of the intended task.

r002.rationale: The response says pilots use simulators to rehearse skills and mentally correct for approximations, but it does not clearly distinguish practicing to fly in the real world from practicing to master the simulator itself.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key difference is what each of them brings to the simulator. When a human pilot sits down in a flight simulator, they're not learning to perceive the world from scratch. They already know what a horizon looks like, what it means for something to be moving toward them, how a control surface responds to force. They have decades of embodied experience with physics, with objects, with their own body. The simulator is really just teaching them a fairly narrow skill on top of an enormous foundation of prior knowledge. And because of that, the simulator doesn't have to be perfect. The pilot can look at a slightly cartoonish rendering of a runway and fill in the gaps with everything they already know. The things the simulator gets wrong are mostly things the pilot already understands well enough to correct for.

For a robot learning from simulated data, the situation has historically been almost exactly reversed. The robot often doesn't have that foundation. If you train a policy purely in simulation, the simulation isn't just teaching the skill, it's teaching what the world is. So every imperfection in the simulator, every way the lighting is a little off or the contact physics are a little wrong or the objects don't quite deform the way real objects do, that becomes part of the robot's model of reality. It has no way to know which parts are artifacts and which parts are real. That's really what the sim-to-real gap is. It's not that simulators are bad, it's that the learner has nothing else to lean on.

So I think the interesting question isn't really "simulation versus real data," it's "what does the learner already know when it enters the simulator." And this is where things have been changing. If you start with a model that has been trained on a lot of real-world data, whether that's internet-scale video, or real robot experience, or language, then it starts to look a lot more like the human pilot. It already has a notion of what objects are and how scenes are structured, and now simulation can play the role it plays for people, which is a place to practice a specific skill cheaply and safely, especially the rare or dangerous situations you don't want to encounter for the first time in the real world. In that regime, the simulator doesn't have to be a substitute for reality. It just has to be good enough to exercise the particular thing you care about, and the model's prior knowledge handles the rest.

There's also a subtler point about what humans actually learn in the simulator. A lot of what a pilot practices is procedural and decision-level: what to do when an engine fails, how to sequence a checklist under stress. Those things transfer well because they don't depend much on fine perceptual details. The low-level stuff, the feel of the controls, is mostly learned in the real aircraft. I think a mature version of robot learning will probably look similar, where simulation is heavily used for the parts that are abstract and combinatorial, and real-world experience is still essential for the parts that depend on the messy details of contact and perception. The mistake is treating simulation as a uniform replacement for experience rather than as one source of data that's good for some things and weak for others.

r001.rationale: The response discusses prior knowledge from real-world data, but does not state that a model trained across multiple domains lacks inherent knowledge of its intended task.

r002.rationale: It explains how simulator practice can transfer to real-world flying, but does not contrast that approach with practicing to master the simulation itself.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is what the learner brings into the simulator. A human pilot already knows an enormous amount about the world. They understand objects, motion, cause and effect. They can read the flight manual and understand an instructor’s explanation. The simulator is teaching them a fairly narrow set of skills on top of that foundation.

When we train a robot in simulation, we often ask it to learn much more of the problem from scratch. And then we’re surprised that it exploits some inaccurate detail of the simulator, or that it fails when the images look different in the real world. But it doesn’t necessarily have the background knowledge to distinguish the aspects of the simulation that matter from the aspects that are incidental.

For example, a human wouldn’t generally conclude that a particular texture on the simulator’s display is essential to flying the airplane. A learned policy might use that texture if it predicts something useful during training. That’s a perfectly reasonable solution to the problem we actually gave it, even if it isn’t the solution we intended.

So I wouldn’t frame this as humans being able to learn from simulation and robots being unable to. The question is what prior experience makes simulation useful, and what you’re trying to learn there. If a robot already has a broad foundation of real-world experience, simulation could serve a role much closer to the one it serves for a human pilot: a place to practice particular skills, including situations that would be expensive or dangerous to encounter in reality.

r001.rationale: The response says a robot may lack background knowledge to separate useful simulator features from incidental ones, but it does not state that models trained on multiple domains do not inherently know their intended task.

r002.rationale: The response distinguishes practicing particular skills from learning broadly in simulation, but it does not clearly compare the learning approach for real-world flying with the approach for mastering the simulation itself.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting difference is what the learner brings into the simulator. A human pilot is not learning from scratch. They already have a visual system, they understand objects and motion, and they have a lot of experience with the physical world. They’re using the simulator to acquire a relatively specific set of skills on top of that foundation.

With a robot, we often ask the simulation to provide much more of the learning. And then the robot can exploit things that are true in the simulator but aren’t true in reality. Maybe the contact dynamics are a little different, or there’s some visual feature that makes the task artificially easy. If your objective is just to get a high reward in simulation, there’s no reason for the model to avoid those shortcuts.

Of course, humans can learn bad habits in simulators too. So I wouldn’t draw a fundamental distinction there. The question is whether the simulator captures the aspects of the task that you need to learn, and whether the learner has enough grounding to deal with the aspects it doesn’t capture. As robotic models acquire more experience in the real world, I think simulation can play a role much closer to the role it plays for a human pilot: a place to practice particular situations, rather than the place where you have to learn everything about how the world works.

r001.rationale: The response discusses simulator learning and real-world grounding, but says nothing about models trained across multiple domains lacking knowledge of their intended task.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a human pilot using simulation to practice specific skills for the real world with optimizing reward within the simulation, describing different learning approaches.
